subject: English
central_question: How does the story use satire and dramatic irony to show that arrogance, political power and human cruelty cannot control fate?
in_scope_units: Before you read: human attitudes towards wild animals.
Section I: the Tiger King’s grand titles, announced death, miraculous infant speech and astrological prophecy.
Section II: English upbringing, accession to power, first tiger and warning about the hundredth tiger.
Section III: hunting monopoly, danger to the throne, British officer and the diamond-ring solution.
Section IV: extinction of local tigers, a politically chosen marriage and the rise of the tally to ninety-nine.
Section V: the missing hundredth tiger, the dewan’s old tiger, the missed shot and the hunters’ concealment.
The wooden tiger, infection, operation and the Maharaja’s ironic death.
Reading with Insight Questions 1–5 on satire, dramatic irony, minions, wildlife and ecological care.
banned_topics: Scientific evaluation of astrology beyond its satirical use in the story.
A general history of princely states or the Indian National Congress beyond references in the narrative.
Current wildlife cases not supplied in the chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: The Maharaja personally kills the hundredth living tiger.
known_pitfalls.correction: His shot misses; the tiger faints and a hunter later kills it.

known_pitfalls.claim: The prophecy is defeated when ninety-nine tigers are killed.
known_pitfalls.correction: The wooden tiger causes the fatal infection and becomes the ironic hundredth tiger.

known_pitfalls.claim: The British officer wants only to protect wildlife.
known_pitfalls.correction: He wants to hunt or at least pose with a dead tiger, and the episode satirises imperial privilege.

known_pitfalls.claim: The Maharaja’s officials obey because they admire his wisdom.
known_pitfalls.correction: Their reactions repeatedly show fear of losing jobs, property or position.

recommended_example_progression: Use Reading with Insight Q1 to trace satire and dramatic irony from prophecy to death.
Use Reading with Insight Q2 to examine the treatment of innocent animals.
Use Reading with Insight Q3 to analyse the Maharaja’s minions and rule by fear.
Use the embedded Read and find out prompts to follow the changing hundred-tiger plan.
Finish with Reading with Insight Q5 on care for Earth and all life.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The story ends with Reading with Insight Questions 1–5 on dramatic irony, cruelty to animals, fearful obedience, game hunting and an ecological system of care.
